Two patients had tumor pathology (Patient 2 and Pa-
tient 5). Immunohistochemistry showed positive for
GAD65 antibody in the thymic cysts in Patient 5 but neg-
ative in the breast tissue in Patient 2 (Fig. 1).
All patients showed positive for GAD65 antibody in
the CSF. The CSF of Patient 1 showed strongly positive in
the tissue sections of rat hippocampus and cerebellum
(Fig. 2a1). The CBA showed strongly positive for GAD
antibody in the CSF of Patient 1. The GAD antibody of

cases.text:
Patient 2 was not obvious in the rat hippocampal-tissue
section but was strongly positive on CBA. There was no
positive detection of any of the other autoimmune anti-
bodies, i.e., Ma2, Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2 (CRMP5), and Amphi-
physin antibodies.
Four patients (80%) had abnormal MRI findings, and
the results for Patient 1 suggested that she had significant
lesions in the bilateral hippocampus (Fig. 2a4). Patient 3
was found to have blurred vision, occasionally with a brief
episode of diplopia, a feeling of abnormality on the right
side of the face (like ants crawling on her skin); no spe-
cific syndrome was identified and there was no obvious
reason for her symptoms. All patients received immuno-
therapy (Table 1, specific immunotherapy regimens) and
all experienced a significant improvement, although 4 of
5 had recurrence of disease after the treatment.
Discussion
The most common GAD antibody-related neurological
disease is SPS, followed by cerebellar ataxia, refractory epi-
lepsy, limbic encephalitis, and extralimbic encephalitis [2,
6]. GAD antibody-related autoimmune myelitis is very
rare; the only reports in the literature are of its appearance
along with pancreatic tumors [1] and our previous study
[4]. Interestingly, in this study, there was a variety of clini-
cal manifestations, even though it was a small cohort. There
were cases of SPS, encephalitis, myelitis, painful paralysis,
decreased vision, and paresthesia. This indicates the het -
erogeneity of clinical manifestations in patients with neu-
rological diseases associated with GAD65 antibodies.
In patients positive for GAD antibodies, SPS is the
most common neurological syndrome. At the same time,
typical SPS-related tumors are breast cancer and thymo-
ma, accounting for 53% of tumors, and 75% of them re-
spond to treatment. However, there is no evidence that
thymoma cells express GAD65 or GAD67 [7]. In the thy-
mic cysts of Patient 5, expression of GAD65 was found in
thymoma cells. On the other hand, although the presence
of GAD antibodies is usually associated with nonpara-
neoplastic forms of zombie syndrome and cerebellar
ataxia associated with multiple endocrine autoimmunity
[1], there was negative expression in the breast tissue in
Patient 2 who had GAD antibody-positive breast cancer.
The mechanism of GAD antibody development may be
paraneoplastic or autoimmune. At present, it has been re-
ported in the literature that GAD expressed by tumors may
immunize mature T cells and B cells, thereby activating
humoral and cellular immunity [8]. On the other hand,
Chang et al. [3] claimed that although GAD is an intracel-
lular protein, it may be exposed to extracellular humoral
immunity during the exocytosis of GABAergic neurons,
thus inducing specific cellular-humoral immunity.

cases.text:
Patient 5 had autoimmune myelitis with thymoma and
was GAD antibody-positive [4]. After resection of the
thymus mass, histopathological examination confirmed a
benign thymic cyst; further immunohistochemistry
showed positive for the expression of GAD65 in the thy-
mic cysts. Interestingly, in Patient 2, who had SPS with
breast cancer and GAD antibodies, the tumor cells did
not express GAD antibodies. We believe that the GAD
expressed in the peripheral tissues as a potential immune
antigen may be used as an immune-activating agent to
stimulate specific cellular and humoral immunity and
produce specific GAD antibodies. Furthermore, T cells
attack the tissues of the central nervous system (CNS) that
also express GAD antigen, and this leads to the occur-
rence of disease [1, 8].
We noted that the indirect immunofluorescence pat-
tern of Patient 1 and Patient 2 showed a significant differ-
ence in fluorescence: the rat hippocampal-tissue section
of Patient 1 was strongly positive and that of Patient 2 was
weakly positive. At the same time, in the cerebellar-tissue
sections, the CSF was positive for GAD antibody for both
patients. CBA confirmed that the GAD antibody was
strongly positive. The difference in fluorescence pattern
could be due to the different affinity of the GAD65 anti-
body in the hippocampus. Antibodies derived from dif-
ferent patients may be structurally different isomers, and
thus there is a difference in the affinity in the hippocam-
pus. The tissue affinity of antibodies with different iso-
mers is different, and the degree of injury in the attacked
brain tissue region is also different; this is what leads to
different clinical characteristics in different patients.
We can also confirm the brain tissue area of GAD an-
tibody attack from the perspective of imaging. Corre-
spondingly, in the MRI results of GAD antibody for pa-
tients with a high affinity in the rat hippocampal tissue,
we found that the bilateral hippocampal area of the pa-
tient showed a low-density shadow, suggesting damage in

the bilateral hippocampus. Nakajima et al. [9] measured
the antibody affinity of GAD antibody in children with
diabetes mellitus. It was found that the responsiveness of
GAD antibody was usually heterogeneous, and differenc-
es in antibody response may stem from different immune
events. Children with multiple islet autoantibodies or di-
abetes have always had high-affinity GADAs [10].
On the other hand, the heterogeneity of clinical fea-
tures can also be explained by differences in epitope rec-
ognition of GAD antibodies. In the study by Vianello et
al. [11], the hippocampal cells of fetal rats were cultured
in vitro with the serum of GAD antibody-positive epilep-
tic patients, SPS patients, and ataxia patients. They ob-
served that the serum of GAD-related epileptic patients
had strong immunoreactivity. Although the serum of pa-
tients with ataxia and SPS also showed responsiveness,
the labeling patterns were significantly different. This in-
dicates that there is different epitope recognition of GAD
antibodies. Further experimental studies of hippocampal
tissue affinity of GAD antibodies are necessary.
Although different combinations of immunotherapy
were used, all patients responded to therapy. Interesting-
ly, 4 patients developed disease recurrence including both
patients with thymic abnormalities, and Patient 5 used
the immunosuppressive agent AZA. This suggests that
patients with GAD65 antibodies, especially those with an
abnormal thymic gland, should be followed up continu-
ously, and patients with GAD antibody-positive CNS dis-
ease should receive immunotherapy in a timely manner.
In summary, our study reported clinical heterogeneity
in patients with positive GAD antibodies. The occurrence
of GAD antibody-associated CNS disease may be related
to the high affinity of antibodies in the hippocampus re-
gion. Immunotherapy has obvious effects in patients pos-
itive for GAD antibodies, and the early application of im-
munotherapy can have an impact on prognosis.
